author: EmuCore - Hub
title: Restore EmuCoreX library access after an Android update
summary: Reconnect the exact PS2 library tree through Android's Storage Access Framework, distinguish a revoked permission from a missing SD card, avoid duplicate roots, and prove that access survives a reboot before removing anything.
heroAlt: Android Developers page explaining the Storage Access Framework and ACTION_OPEN_DOCUMENT_TREE folder picker

blocks.text: Confirm that Android lost the tree grant

After an Android or vendor-system update, an EmuCoreX library can look empty even though every personal disc image is still present. First open the system Files app and browse to the old library folder. If the folder itself is missing, the SD card or USB device is not mounted and granting permission again cannot fix it. If Files can open the folder but EmuCoreX reports the root as unavailable, the likely fault is the document-tree permission that connects the app to that provider.

Do not delete the library entry, move game images, clear app data, or create a second folder yet. None of those actions repairs a revoked Storage Access Framework grant, and each one can make existing favorites or per-game profiles harder to match.
Record the old root before opening the picker

items: Take a screenshot of the unavailable-folder row and its displayed storage name.
Count the personal game images in the physical folder with the system Files app; exclude archives, partial copies, and backup subfolders.
Write down whether the root is on internal storage, a removable SD card, a USB provider, or a cloud-backed provider.
Back up the active EmuCoreX emulator-data folder separately. Re-authorizing a game folder should not modify memory cards, but the backup protects against unrelated cleanup mistakes.
If the volume is removable, eject and remount it once through Android before changing any EmuCoreX entry.

blocks.text: Select the same document tree, not a nearby path

items: 1. Open the EmuCoreX library-folder manager and choose the action for adding or reconnecting a game folder.
2. In Android's picker, use the provider list to select the same physical storage recorded earlier. Similar folder names under Internal storage and an SD card are different document trees.

3. Browse to the existing PS2 library root. Select the folder that directly contains the organized game subfolders or images; do not select one ISO and do not select a parent that also contains backups.
4. Choose Use this folder, or the equivalent confirmation supplied by the device, and approve access when Android shows the warning dialog.
5. Return to EmuCoreX and run one manual library refresh. Wait for scanning and metadata work to finish instead of repeatedly pressing refresh.

6. Compare the resulting entry count with the physical count you recorded. Multidisc sets and unsupported files explain legitimate differences; two entries for every title indicate an overlapping root.
7. Cold-start one personally dumped game from the restored root, then close EmuCoreX normally.

blocks.text: The Android picker returns a content URI, not a conventional filesystem path. EmuCoreX asks Android to retain read access to that URI, while the document provider decides how the volume and folder are represented. A card replacement, filesystem repair, work-profile change, or provider migration can produce a new URI even when the visible folder name is unchanged. This is why selecting by storage identity and contents matters more than typing or remembering a path.
Prove that the restored permission is persistent

items: Force-stop EmuCoreX from Android settings, reopen it, and launch the same test game without adding the folder again.
Restart Android with the removable volume inserted, wait for the system to mount it, and verify that the library root becomes available.
Favorite one test entry, refresh once, and confirm that the favorite remains attached to the same title and region.
Open a title from another library root, if one exists, to prove that the repair did not replace unrelated permissions.
Leave the old files in place until both the post-force-stop and post-reboot checks pass.

blocks.text: Remove an accidental duplicate without touching files

If re-authorization creates duplicate entries, inspect the selected roots before deleting anything in Android. The common cause is that both a parent and its child are scanned, or that the old unavailable URI and a new working URI point at the same content. Remove only the newly added root from EmuCoreX, refresh once, and observe which entries remain. If the working entries disappear, re-add the exact root and retire the stale permission instead. File deletion is never part of this rollback.
Symptoms that permission repair will not solve

items: The system Files app cannot open the SD card: inspect the card, adapter, filesystem, and Android mount state before using EmuCoreX.
Only one image freezes at the same sector: verify that personal dump rather than replacing the entire tree permission.
The picker shows a cloud placeholder instead of local bytes: make the image locally available or use stable local storage for the test.
Access works until the USB cable moves: power delivery or the physical connection is unstable.
A work-profile or multi-user switch hides the provider: grants belong to the Android user or profile that selected the tree.

blocks.text: Rollback when the new grant makes the library worse

Return to the folder manager, remove only the grant added during this procedure, and refresh once. Reinsert or remount the original volume, then reselect the recorded root if it was healthy. Restore the emulator-data backup only if a separate operation actually changed profiles or saves; a folder grant failure alone does not justify overwriting memory cards. Keep the screenshots and counts until the library survives another reboot.
